title: A rank-one reductive group as an explicit semidirect quotient
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field] [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $H$ be a split reductive affine $F$-group scheme with a split maximal torus $T$ [def-sc-group-scheme] [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Suppose its root set is $\{\gamma,-\gamma\}$, with root subgroups and canonical coroot $\gamma^\vee:\mathbf G_m\to T$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Here $\mathbf G_a(A)=(A,+)$ and $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for each commutative $F$-algebra $A$. Write $\operatorname{SL}_2(A)=\{M\in\operatorname{Mat}_{2\times2}(A):\det M=1\}$, $d(s)=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})$, and $x_+(a)=I_2+aE_{12}$, $x_-(a)=I_2+aE_{21}$. Let $v:\operatorname{SL}_2\to H$ be a group-scheme homomorphism restricting to isomorphisms $x_+(\mathbf G_a)\xrightarrow{\sim}U_\gamma$ and $x_-(\mathbf G_a)\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{-\gamma}$ and satisfying $v(d(s))=\gamma^\vee(s)$ over every $A$. Define $C_\gamma(t)(M)=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma(t),1)M\operatorname{diag}(\gamma(t)^{-1},1)$. Let $E_\gamma$ be the affine scheme $\operatorname{SL}_2\times_FT$ with multiplication
$$(M,t)(N,u)=(M C_\gamma(t)(N),tu).$$
Then $E_\gamma$ is an affine $F$-group scheme of finite type, and
$$\pi_\gamma:E_\gamma\longrightarrow H,\qquad (M,t)\longmapsto v(M)t$$
is a group-scheme homomorphism whose coordinate-algebra map is faithfully flat (extension of scalars is exact and detects zero modules). Its scheme-theoretic kernel is isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m$ by the map
$$k_\gamma:\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{\sim}\ker\pi_\gamma,\qquad s\longmapsto(d(s),\gamma^\vee(s)^{-1}).$$
In particular, for every $A$, one has
$$v(C_\gamma(t)(M))=t v(M)t^{-1}\qquad(t\in T(A),\ M\in\operatorname{SL}_2(A)).$$
There is no restriction on $\dim T$ or on the characteristic, and all kernel and equivariance assertions are identities of scheme morphisms, not merely statements on $F$-points.

source.place: Proposition 20.32 and Theorem 20.33 with Corollary 20.34, printed pp.418--419; Theorem 21.11 and paragraphs 21.23--21.24, printed pp.429--432. Agent formulation of the semidirect presentation underlying these matrix models; retain the semisimple-rank-one hypothesis and the corrected derived groups.

proof.text:
Put $u_\pm=v\circ x_\pm$. The root parametrization theorem gives $t u_+(z)t^{-1}=u_+(\gamma(t)z)$ and $t u_-(z)t^{-1}=u_-(\gamma(t)^{-1}z)$ over every test algebra. These are exactly the conjugation formulas for $C_\gamma(t)$ on $x_\pm$. On $d(s)$ both actions fix $v(d(s))=\gamma^\vee(s)$, because $T$ is commutative. These checks imply equivariance on all of $\operatorname{SL}_2$, as follows. Write $M$ with entries $M_{11}=a,M_{12}=b,M_{21}=c,M_{22}=e$, with $ae-bc=1$, and $w=x_+(-1)x_-(1)x_+(-1)$. The two principal opens $D(a),D(c)$ cover, since $1=ae-bc\in(a,c)$. On them, respectively, direct multiplication gives
$$M=x_-(c/a)d(a)x_+(b/a),\qquad M=x_+(a/c)w d(c)x_+(e/c).$$
Thus equivariance holds on both opens, including on $w$ by its displayed word in $x_\pm$. Equality of morphisms can be checked on this open cover, also after product with $T$. This proves the required identity as a scheme-morphism identity, without assuming that elementary matrices generate $\operatorname{SL}_2(A)$ globally.

source.place: 21.19, formula (135), and 21.24, pp.431--432; explicit two-chart matrix calculation.

proof.text:
Conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(\gamma(t),1)$ preserves determinant and defines an algebraic action: $C_\gamma(tu)=C_\gamma(t)C_\gamma(u)$ and $C_\gamma(1)=1$. The multiplication specified in the statement is therefore associative, with identity $(I_2,1)$ and inverse
$$(M,t)^{-1}=(C_\gamma(t^{-1})(M^{-1}),t^{-1}).$$
All maps are regular: matrix inversion in determinant one is the adjugate, and $\gamma(t)^{-1}$ is a character of the torus. The underlying scheme is affine of finite type: its coordinate algebra is the tensor product of $F[a,b,c,e]/(ae-bc-1)$ with a Laurent polynomial algebra for the split torus. Finally Step 1 gives
$$\pi_\gamma((M,t)(N,u))=v(M)t v(N)t^{-1}tu=\pi_\gamma(M,t)\pi_\gamma(N,u).$$
Thus $E_\gamma$ and $\pi_\gamma$ have the asserted group-scheme structures.

source.place: Agent construction of the semidirect group law from the action in 21.19 and 21.24, pp.431--432.

proof.text:
Let $n=v(w)\in H(F)$. For $q=\gamma(t)$ the matrix identity $C_\gamma(t)(w)=d(q)w$, together with Step 1, gives
$$n t n^{-1}=t\gamma^\vee(\gamma(t)^{-1}).$$
This belongs to $T$ over every test algebra and is an automorphism there (its square is the identity, using $\gamma\circ\gamma^\vee(s)=s^2$). Hence $n$ normalizes $T$. Applying $\gamma$ shows that its Weyl action interchanges $\gamma$ and $-\gamma$. Choose $B=P(\gamma^\vee)$ by the regular-cocharacter Borel theorem: its positive roots are precisely $\{\gamma\}$, since the two integer character pairings are $2,-2$, even in characteristic two. The root-product coordinates identify its unipotent radical with $U_\gamma$, and the Borel-pair theorem gives $B=U_\gamma\rtimes T$. The Bruhat-chart theorem now identifies the class of $n$ with $w_0$, because it reverses this positive-root system. In particular,
$$B\cap nBn^{-1}=T,$$
and $(z,b_0)\mapsto u_+(z)n b_0$ is an open immersion with dense image.

Translate the last open immersion on the left by $n^{-1}$. The identity $w^{-1}x_+(z)w=x_-(-z)$ identifies its first factor with $U_{-\gamma}$. Replace its $B$ factor by $T\times U_\gamma$: the Borel product isomorphism $U_\gamma\times T\simeq B$ can be reordered by $u t=t(t^{-1}ut)$, with inverse given by the same conjugation formula. Consequently
$$j: \mathbf G_a\times T\times\mathbf G_a\longrightarrow H,\qquad (z,t_0,y)\longmapsto u_-(z)t_0u_+(y)$$
is an isomorphism onto an open subscheme $\Omega$ containing $T$. In particular these three coordinates are unique over every test algebra; this uses the stated scheme-theoretic Bruhat open immersion, not uniqueness only on field-valued points.

source.place: Theorem 21.84 and Summary 21.86, pp.451--452; translate the longest-cell chart of Theorem 21.73.

proof.text:
Apply the affine homomorphism flat-image theorem to the homomorphism $\pi_\gamma:E_\gamma\to H$ constructed in Step 2. Its hypotheses require only affine finite-type group schemes over a field, already verified; write its factorization as $E_\gamma\to I\hookrightarrow H$, with the first coordinate-algebra map faithfully flat. The inclusions of $T,U_\gamma,U_{-\gamma}$ into $H$ all factor through $I$: lift them to $E_\gamma$ by $t\mapsto(I_2,t)$ and $z\mapsto(x_\pm(z),1)$. The reductive rank-one tangent decomposition states
$$\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\mathfrak h_\gamma\oplus\mathfrak h_{-\gamma}.$$
The root parametrization theorem identifies the last two spaces with the tangent spaces of $U_\gamma,U_{-\gamma}$. These three closed subgroups are smooth and connected. The smooth-subgroup tangent-generation theorem, applied to their inclusions and to the arbitrary closed subgroup $I$, yields $I=H$. Thus the coordinate-algebra map of $\pi_\gamma$ is faithfully flat as claimed.

source.place: Theorem 5.39, p.108 (affine algebra formulation from Theorem 3.31, pp.73--74); Corollary 10.17, p.191; Theorem 21.11(b),(f), pp.428--430, and 21.23, p.432.

proof.text:
We next locate the entire scheme-theoretic kernel in the matrix chart $D(a)$. First $n\notin B(K)$ for any algebraically closed extension $K/F$: otherwise $nB_Kn^{-1}=B_K$, while the scheme intersection in Step 3 would force $B_K=T_K$, contradicting $B_K=U_{\gamma,K}\rtimes T_K$ with $U_{\gamma,K}\simeq\mathbf G_{a,K}$. If $a=0$ for a matrix over such a $K$, then $c\ne0$ and the second chart formula in Step 1 gives
$$v(M)=n\gamma^\vee(c)u_+(e/c)\in nB(K).$$
It cannot belong to $T(K)\subseteq B(K)$. Now take any commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and $(M,t)\in\ker\pi_\gamma(A)$. If $a$ were a nonunit, a maximal ideal containing it followed by an algebraic closure of the residue field would produce the forbidden matrix with $a=0$ and $v(M)=t^{-1}\in T$. Therefore $a\in A^\times$. This argument excludes only the complement of the chart; it makes no reducedness assumption on $A$ or on the kernel. Equivalently the kernel morphism to $\operatorname{SL}_2$ factors through the open $D(a)$.

source.place: Theorem 21.84, pp.451--452, and 21.24, p.432; explicit chart exclusion using the scheme-theoretic opposite-Borel intersection.

proof.text:
For the same arbitrary $A$, use the first matrix chart and $v(M)=t^{-1}$:
$$u_-(c/a)\gamma^\vee(a)u_+(b/a)=t^{-1}.$$
The open-chart isomorphism $j$ of Step 4 compares this with the coordinates $(0,t^{-1},0)$. It gives $c/a=b/a=0$ and $\gamma^\vee(a)=t^{-1}$. Thus $b=c=0$, $e=a^{-1}$ and
$$(M,t)=(d(a),\gamma^\vee(a)^{-1}).$$
Conversely every displayed pair has image $1$. Its product with the corresponding pair for $s'$ is $(d(as'),\gamma^\vee(as')^{-1})$, since diagonal conjugation fixes diagonal matrices. Thus $k_\gamma$ is a homomorphism. It is a regular map into the kernel; its inverse is the regular invertible coordinate $a$ on the kernel chart $D(a)$. The two composites are identities by the calculations over arbitrary $A$, giving the required isomorphism of group schemes. The scheme-coordinate comparison, rather than the geometric-point exclusion alone, proves the kernel equality on nilpotent test algebras.
